rows.title: 'Welcome to the USA! Now get to work.'
rows.standfirst: When refugees arrive in the U.S. the clock starts ticking. They usually have up to 90 days to get a job and become 'self-sufficient'.

rows.title: Philanthropies pledge $500 million to address 'crisis in local news'
rows.standfirst: The new coalition of donors, led by the MacArthur Foundation, says one out of every five Americans lives in a "news desert" with little to no reliable local news.

rows.title: Biden wants federal workforce to come to the office more. Some ask why?
rows.standfirst: As employers including the federal government cut back on remote work, employees who never had any intention of working from an office push back and threaten to retire or resign.

rows.title: Dear Life Kit: My husband shuts down any time I try to talk about our finances
rows.standfirst: I'm struggling to get my husband to make a family budget with me. Whenever the topic comes up, he completely gets defensive. How do I get him to talk to me about money?

rows.title: Why autoworkers are asking for a 46% pay raise
rows.standfirst: Bold union demands, bolstered by a tight labor market and frustration throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, are paying off in some sectors with significant raises for workers.

rows.title: The dementia tax
rows.standfirst: More than 7 million Americans are living with dementia. To take care of this population, family members must often make the difficult choice of giving up work or paying for a costly facility. Today on the show, the rising cost of memory care in an aging population.

rows.title: The Andy Warhol Supreme Court case and what it means for the future of art
rows.standfirst: In 1981, photographer Lynn Goldsmith took a portrait of the musician Prince. It's a pretty standard headshot — it's in black-and-white, and Prince is staring down the camera lens.

rows.title: When Big Oil Gets In The Carbon Removal Game, Who Wins?
rows.standfirst: Giant machines sucking carbon dioxide out of the air to fight climate change sounds like science fiction, but it's close to becoming a reality, with billions of dollars of support from the U.S. government.

rows.title: 'You could be the hero': Fran Drescher tells NPR how the Hollywood strikes can end
rows.standfirst: Fran Drescher, president of the actors' union SAG-AFTRA, says the Hollywood strikes are at an inflection point.

rows.title: From snow globes to tutoring, strikes kick Hollywood side hustles into high gear
rows.standfirst: One comedy writer opened a snow globe business on Etsy. A showrunner's assistant is offering bar and bat mitzvah tutoring. As the strikes wear on, here's how Hollywood workers are getting by.

rows.title: The perilous hunt for PPP fraud and the hot tip that wasn't
rows.standfirst: The public data on PPP loans contains a lot of suspicious patterns, but it can also send people on wild goose chases

rows.title: Google Turns 25
rows.standfirst: Google was founded 25 years ago by two Stanford PhD students, Larry Page and Sergei Brin.

rows.title: The Beigie Awards: China Edition
rows.standfirst: The Beigies are back, with a twist!

rows.title: NPR CEO John Lansing will leave in December, capping a tumultuous year
rows.standfirst: President and CEO John Lansing plans to leave NPR nine months before his term is set to expire. His tenure has been defined by the pandemic, a racial reckoning, and economic headwinds.

rows.title: Tired of 'circling back' and 'touching base'? How to handle all the workplace jargon
rows.standfirst: Two recent surveys reveal white-collar workers' least favorite corporate clichés, from 'circling back' to 'moving the needle.' Here's why workplace jargon bothers us — and what we can do about it.

rows.title: Autoworkers are on the verge of a historic strike
rows.standfirst: Less than two hours before the strike deadline, United Auto Workers revealed the first wave of plants to be targeted if the union and the Big 3 automakers fail to reach a deal just before midnight.

rows.title: In an effort to make rides safer, Lyft launches Women+ Connect
rows.standfirst: The new opt-in feature lets women and nonbinary drivers prioritize passengers who fit the same description. But it's not a guarantee and is only available in a handful of cities for now.

rows.title: Wait — did we really need to raise rates?
rows.standfirst: Inflation remains stubbornly high as the Federal Open Markets Committee weighs whether they will raise interest rates again. However, new research suggests that elevated interest rates weren't the primary driver for the decline in inflation. Today, we take a look at the debate surrounding disinflation and what comes next for the Federal Reserve.

rows.title: Exxon minimized climate change internally after conceding that fossil fuels cause it
rows.standfirst: The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that as recently as 2016, Exxon executives were privately pushing back on the idea that humans need to cut their use of oil and gas to limit global warming.

rows.title: Here's where things stand just before the UAW and Big 3 automakers' contract deadline
rows.standfirst: The union is prepared to strike. Auto companies say they're still waiting for counteroffers. And so far, there's no deal in sight.

rows.title: Now's your chance to solve a crossword puzzle with Natasha Lyonne
rows.standfirst: Want Adam Scott to walk your dog? What about dinner with Bob Odenkirk? Some of Hollywood's most beloved names are auctioning off unique experiences to help support the writers' strike

rows.title: HBO's 'Real Time with Bill Maher' to return during Writers Guild strike
rows.standfirst: Maher posted on X that he won't have any written segments. But since Maher is himself a writer, it will be difficult for the show to go ahead "without a violation of WGA strike rules," says the Guild.

rows.title: What a crop of upcoming IPOs from Birkenstock to Instacart tells us about the economy
rows.standfirst: A crop of IPOs are coming, starting with chip designer Arm, which is making its debut on Thursday. It's another sign of confidence in markets — and the U.S. economy.

rows.title: The UAW unveils major plan if talks with Big 3 automakers fail: The 'stand up strike'
rows.standfirst: The United Auto Workers could strike at targeted auto plants before expanding the walkouts to additional locations if the union and the Detroit Three automakers fail to reach a new contract.

rows.title: Giant vacuums and other government climate bets
rows.standfirst: Yesterday we brought you a debate over whether the government should subsidize industries in the name of economic growth and societal benefits. Today on the show, we zero in on the climate industrial policy of the Biden administration, which is funneling billions into experimental projects that promise to remove, capture and store carbon. It's an effort by the U.S. to meet its ambitious climate goals, but it's not without its skeptics.

rows.title: China's weakening economy in two Indicators
rows.standfirst: In China, data on the economy is sometimes difficult to come by. The Chinese government has put a pause on releasing some of its official economic data. But many of the stories emerging from the country paint a clear picture: the second largest economy in the world is struggling.

rows.title: 'Oldest start-up on earth': Birkenstock's IPO filing is exactly as you'd expect
rows.standfirst: "We are serving a primal need of all human beings," Birkenstock's CEO writes to prospective shareholders. "We are a footbed company selling the experience of walking as intended by nature."

rows.title: How Concerns Over EVs are Driving the UAW Towards a Strike
rows.standfirst: The president of the United Auto Workers says the union is planning to carry out sudden, strategic and partial strikes at plants should contract talks with Detroit's Big Three automakers fail ahead of a contract deadline on Thursday night.

rows.title: Sky-high CEO pay is in focus as workers everywhere are demanding higher wages
rows.standfirst: As autoworkers' real wages fall, top executives at the Big Three carmakers continue to earn tens of millions of dollars each year — hundreds of times more than the median employee.

rows.title: The who's who of the tech world meet with senators to debate plan to regulate AI
rows.standfirst: More than 20 business leaders and others, including tech titans Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, are on Capitol Hill to meet with U.S. senators.

rows.title: Selling safety in the fight against wildfires
rows.standfirst: Wildfires are becoming more frequent and serious due to human-caused climate change. This is prompting a new industry focused on residential wildfire preparedness. Today, we consider the new technology addressing wildfire risk and the cost of protecting yourself.

rows.title: Anheuser-Busch says it will no longer amputate the tails of Budweiser's Clydesdales
rows.standfirst: The beermaker says it will end the practice known as tail docking after it came under pressure by animal rights group PETA.

rows.title: 2 Black TikTok workers claim discrimination: Both were fired after complaining to HR
rows.standfirst: Two Black employees bring charges with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, alleging they suffered discrimination and retaliation while working at the social media giant.

rows.title: Fox founder Rupert Murdoch steps down from his media empire, handing it to his son
rows.standfirst: Rupert Murdoch is stepping down as chair of his media empire, which includes Fox News, The Wall Street Journal and The New York Post. He is handing the reins to his son Lachlan.

rows.title: Kraft is recalling some American cheese slices over potential choking hazard
rows.standfirst: The company said one of its wrapping machines developed a temporary issue that makes it possible for a thin strip of film to remain on the slice even after it's been removed from the wrapper.

rows.title: "Based on a true story"
rows.standfirst: When a group of amateur investors rallied around the stock for GameStop back in 2021, the story blew up the internet. News outlets around the world, including us here at Planet Money, rushed in to explain why the stock for this retail video game company was suddenly skyrocketing, at times by as much as 1700% in value, and what that meant for the rest of us.

rows.title: UAW strike latest: GM sends 2,000 workers home in Kansas
rows.standfirst: General Motors had previously warned it would need to stop production at its Fairfax, Kansas, assembly plant, because it relied on parts that came from a Missouri plant that is currently on strike.

rows.title: The Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady but hints at more action this year
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged Wednesday, despite stubborn inflation, although it left the door open to an additional rate hike in November or December.

rows.title: Having a hard time finding Clorox wipes? Blame it on a cyberattack
rows.standfirst: The Clorox Co. — which also includes brands such as Pine-Sol, Brita, Glad and Burt's Bees — says it's operating at a "lower rate of processing" after an August hack on its IT infrastructure.

rows.title: Fed-up consumers are increasingly going after food companies for misleading claims
rows.standfirst: This week a federal judge in Manhattan allowed a case to move forward against Starbucks over claims its fruit-based drinks were lacking fruit.

rows.title: Why the UAW is fighting so hard for these 4 key demands in the auto strike
rows.standfirst: Driving the UAW's tough stance in negotiations with the Big Three automakers is the sense that the union is owed a long-overdue redressal for all the concessions workers made in 2007.

rows.title: The video game industry is in uproar over a software pricing change. Here's why
rows.standfirst: The Unity Engine, a popular game development tool, is getting a pricing overhaul. Developers are enraged.

rows.title: The Beigie Awards: Manufacturing takes center stage
rows.standfirst: The Beigies roll around once again to recognize the regional Federal Reserve Bank with the best Beige Book entry. This edition's winner put a spotlight on a company increasing their efforts to recruit young people for an important piece of the manufacturing puzzle.

rows.title: Wonder where Hollywood's strikes are headed? Movies might offer a clue
rows.standfirst: Hollywood has churned out films that depict labor organizers as communists, and labor bosses as gangsters. So it should come as no surprise that real-life negotiations with the studios are so tricky.

rows.title: Trump to skip second GOP debate and head to Detroit to court autoworkers instead
rows.standfirst: Former President Donald Trump won't be at the second Republican debate, unsurprisingly. His counter-programming this time involves union autoworkers, engaged in a strike against Detroit automakers.

rows.title: All Onewheel e-skateboards are recalled after reported deaths
rows.standfirst: Future Motion recalled 300,000 boards after previous resistance to the federal safety commission's push for a recall. Four incidents of fatal brain trauma are linked to the self-balancing boards.

rows.title: Janet Yellen says a government shutdown would add to risks of a recession
rows.standfirst: Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen is sounding the alarm about the damage a government shutdown could do to the U.S. economy. "It's really reckless and will impose immediate harm," Yellen told NPR.

rows.title: Some states pick up the tab to keep national parks open during federal shutdown
rows.standfirst: Don't cancel that camping trip just yet: Utah, Arizona, and Colorado state governments will foot the bill to keep some national parks open — and tourist dollars flowing — during the shutdown.

rows.title: Twerking, tote bags, and the top of the charts
rows.standfirst: On this musical edition of Indicators of the Week: Live Nation stops taking a cut of small artists' merchandise sales. Meanwhile, some fans are using the Billboard charts formula to boost their favorite artists to the top. And a Jamaican duo is staking a claim to the famous rhythm that defines Reggaeton. For sponsor-free episodes of The Indicator from Planet Money, subscribe to Planet Money+ via Apple Podcasts or at plus.npr.org.Music by Drop Electric. Find us: TikTok , Instagram , Facebook , Newsletter.

rows.title: Why the Obama era 'car czar' thinks striking autoworkers risk overplaying their hand
rows.standfirst: He was the lead adviser for the Obama administration when the government bailed out auto companies in 2009. Now, he is weighing in on the union strikes against the big 3 American automakers.

rows.title: Trump's N.Y. business empire is 'greatly at risk' from judge's fraud ruling
rows.standfirst: Legal and business experts say the ruling in New York state threatens assets such as Trump Tower and also empowers state Attorney General Letitia James, one of Donald Trump's main legal critics.

rows.title: UAW once again expands its historic strike, hitting two of the Big 3 automakers
rows.standfirst: The United Auto Workers expanded its strike against Ford and GM, but not Stellantis after the company formerly known as Chrysler made last-minute concessions.

rows.title: Have a complaint about CVS? So do pharmacists: Many just walked out
rows.standfirst: After a large walkout forced at least a dozen stores to shut down in the Kansas City area, CVS promises change. But critics say the crisis in staffing and unfair pay extends beyond that market.

rows.title: Overworked and understaffed: Kaiser workers are on the brink of a nationwide strike
rows.standfirst: More than 75,000 Kaiser Permanente health care workers at hundreds of U.S. facilities could go on strike for three days starting Wednesday, in the largest health care strike in the county's history.

rows.title: The White House chief of staff says it's on House Republicans to avert a shutdown
rows.standfirst: Jeff Zients has been getting the White House prepared for the first government shutdown of the Biden administration. Here's what the chief of staff told NPR about it.

rows.title: Fossil fuel rules catch Western towns between old economies and new green goals
rows.standfirst: The Biden administration is trying to dramatically change how and where oil and gas drilling occurs on federal land, which is getting mixed reviews in longtime drilling boom-towns.

rows.title: Here's How a Government Shutdown Could Impact Millions of Americans
rows.standfirst: The federal government will shut down on October 1st if Congress doesn't pass funding legislation for the next fiscal year before then.

rows.title: The walking dead NFTs
rows.standfirst: The NFT mania may have finally run its course. Not too long ago, these pieces of digital art exploded in value with the help of celebrities like Justin Bieber and Paris Hilton. But even the most successful digital artists knew it was a bubble. Today, we consider whether this multi-million dollar fad has truly come to an end or if it's still on its last legs and due for a reimagining.

rows.title: The journey of 'seemingly ranch,' from meme to top of the Empire State Building
rows.standfirst: Heinz and Primal Kitchen are selling limited-edition bottles of "Seemingly Ranch" dressing. The Empire State Building lit up in red and white. It all started, as so many trends do, with Taylor Swift.

rows.title: FTC Chair Lina Khan's lawsuit isn't about breaking up Amazon, for now
rows.standfirst: The FTC's Lina Khan speaks to NPR about the goals of the agency's monopoly lawsuit against Amazon and why she thinks the company unfairly treats sellers on its marketplace.
